strengths: Strong empirical results: 5.09× speedup on ASE while maintaining or improving F1-Score (0.908 vs baseline 0.915), with 43% fewer parameters than SceneScript+MTP
Comprehensive ablation studies (Table 3) systematically validating each component—distance metric variants, parameter sharing, and multiple filtering strategies
Solid technical execution: Task-specific adaptations (distance metric for numerical tokens, parameter-efficient projection blocks) are reasonable and well-motivated for structured prediction
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 2, 7-8) clearly demonstrating inference efficiency gains and filtering strategy analysis
Reproducibility: Implementation details, hyperparameters, and dataset splits provided; results consistent across two datasets (ASE, Structured3D)
Practical value: Significant speedups with maintained accuracy directly address real efficiency constraints in autoregressive models
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Core components (MTP, self-speculative decoding) are from prior work [12, 32, 51]; main contributions are engineering combinations rather than new methods

Incremental CGD contribution: Confidence-guided decoding represents a straightforward refinement over existing scoring-based methods [21, 37]—primarily replacing softmax probability with a learned confidence head (Eq. 4). No ablation comparing alternative confidence formulations

Overstated generalist claims: Paper claims to be 'perception generalist model' with applications to 3D object detection and part reconstruction, but provides zero experimental validation. Evaluation limited to single task despite generalist positioning

Incomplete computational analysis: Insufficient breakdown of speedup sources. Cost of SSD verification pass and confidence computation not analyzed. Latency accounting lacks detail despite 21→3 iteration reduction

Distance metric lacks justification: Simple absolute-difference thresholding (Eq. 3) chosen without exploring alternatives or analyzing appropriateness across varying numerical ranges. Minimal ablation (only τ ∈ {0,2,5})
Missing statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing. Single values reported per condition; differences of 1-2% in F1-score could be within experimental noise

Hyperparameter choices unexplored: Loss weights (λh=0.8, λc=0.5) appear arbitrary; confidence threshold ε sensitivity not analyzed; initialization choice (excluding projection blocks from NTP weights) not validated
No confidence calibration analysis: Binary confidence targets (Eq. 4) not validated for calibration—unclear if predicted confidences reflect actual reliability
Limited scope limits generalizability claims: Both evaluation datasets (ASE, Structured3D) are indoor scenes; evaluation on outdoor or diverse 3D perception domains would strengthen claims

Incomplete baseline comparison: SceneScript+MTP baseline shows surprisingly poor performance (0.815 F1 at n=10 vs 0.915 baseline). Unclear if properly tuned. RoomFormer comparison shows Fast SceneScript slower (230ms vs 54ms), limiting fairness of generalist vs task-specific comparison

strengths: Practical value: Achieves 5.09× speedup on 3D layout estimation while maintaining accuracy, addressing real inference latency problems
Comprehensive experimental validation: Thorough ablation studies (Table 3) and evaluation on two datasets (ASE, Structured3D) with consistent results
Parameter efficiency: Reduces parameter overhead from 69-89% (naive MTP) to 7.5% using shared head mechanism
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with effective figures (Figures 2-4) illustrating the method and comparing inference strategies
Flexible design: Investigates multiple decoding strategies (SSD and CGD) providing different speed-accuracy trade-offs for different use cases
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Primarily combines existing techniques (MTP from [12], SSD from [32,51], confidence-based filtering from [21,37]); the main additions are a straightforward distance metric τ for numerical tokens (Eq. 3) and standard BCE loss for confidence heads (Eq. 4)

Problematic baseline comparison: SceneScript+MTP (Row h, Table 1) achieves only 0.815 F1 vs 0.913 baseline—an 11.04% drop significantly worse than expected from MTP literature, raising concerns about implementation fairness or hyperparameter tuning
Unexplained accuracy improvement: Fast SceneScript (Row i) achieves 12.04% better F1 than baseline despite token filtering; this counterintuitive result warrants investigation but is not explained
Domain-specific scope despite generality claims: Evaluation limited to 3D layout estimation; claims of applicability to object detection and part reconstruction lack any experimental validation

Missing analysis of key findings: (1) Why SSD accepts more tokens (7.46-8.97) than CGD (6.29-7.27) unexplored, (2) Figure 8 showing softmax unreliability lacks deeper investigation of what confidence head learns, (3) Hyperparameter choices (τ=2, λh=0.8, λc=0.5) lack justification

Narrow evaluation scope: Single task evaluation; stated generalization to other 3D perception tasks unsupported by experiments; Structured3D uses ASE pre-training making cross-domain generalization unclear

Missing alternative comparisons: No comparison with knowledge distillation, quantization, pruning, or other inference acceleration methods; limits understanding of whether MTP is optimal for this task

Incomplete architectural details: Distance metric τ application token-dependent or uniform?; Precise projection block architecture beyond '2 feedforward blocks' unclear; confidence head initialization unspecified

strengths: Strong experimental results with 5.09× speedup on ASE while maintaining/improving accuracy and only 7.5% parameter increase, validated on two datasets with comprehensive ablations
Well-motivated practical problem addressing inference bottlenecks in autoregressive structured language models, with thorough analysis demonstrating effectiveness (Figures 2, 7-8)
Comprehensive technical approach combining MTP, token filtering (SSD + CGD), and parameter efficiency with principled design choices (distance metric for numerical tokens, confidence-based filtering)
Excellent experimental rigor including detailed ablations (Table 3), comparison of filtering strategies, qualitative visualizations, and analysis of design choices (softmax score analysis)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and good reproducibility through detailed hyperparameters, training procedures, and implementation details
Sensible adaptation of SSD for structured tasks via distance metrics for numerical tokens, showing 12.04% F1 improvement over naive MTP baseline with significantly fewer parameters
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: MTP and SSD are from prior work; CGD is relatively simple binary classification of token reliability; primary contribution is careful engineering of combinations rather than fundamental innovation

CGD ground truth generation (Eq. 4) creates implicit bias toward first head by using first head predictions in confidence labels; binary boundary classification at τ threshold is crude and misses nuanced reliability information

Incomplete evaluation scope: limited to layout estimation task; claims of 'first MTP application to language-based perception' but generalization to 3D object detection and part reconstruction mentioned in abstract not demonstrated

Practical efficiency claims require nuance: slower than task-specific RoomFormer (230-269ms vs 54ms); speedup advantage primarily over general SceneScript baseline rather than competing efficient methods
Insufficient experimental rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, multiple runs, or statistical significance testing; hyperparameter choices (τ=2, λh=0.8, λc=0.5) lack principled justification

Incomplete analysis: no discussion of failure cases, which layout types benefit most from approach, or when to prefer SSD vs CGD beyond speed/throughput trade-off; τ sensitivity limited despite being key hyperparameter
Parameter-efficient mechanism is straightforward (shared FFN projection blocks), not representing significant methodological contribution beyond standard head-sharing
Missing comparisons with other acceleration techniques (quantization, distillation, batching) and incomplete analysis of confidence head computational overhead during inference

strengths: Strong empirical results with 5.09× speedup on layout estimation and 5.14× on object detection while maintaining or improving accuracy
Comprehensive experimental validation across three datasets (ASE, Structured3D, SceneCAD) with extensive ablation studies (Tables 4, S1-S4)
Well-motivated insight that structured languages are more deterministic and weakly coupled than natural language, enabling feasible multi-token prediction
Novel confidence-guided decoding (CGD) strategy with clever confidence head training based on internal agreement between predictions
Parameter-efficient mechanism reducing parameters by ~48% while maintaining accuracy through head-sharing
Thorough technical soundness with clear adaptation of existing techniques (SSD with distance metrics) to structured language setting
Insightful analysis revealing softmax scores poorly correlate with token reliability (Figures 6-7), an important finding for token filtering
Excellent presentation with clear figures and detailed supplementary material supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (MTP from Gloeckle et al. 2024, SSD from Stern et al. 2018) with task-specific engineering; CGD is relatively straightforward
Tightly coupled to SceneScript and its specific structured language format; unclear generalization to other language-based perception models or different structured languages
Scalability concerns: experiments with n=12, 16 show accuracy degradation; practical limits not established and insufficient analysis of why performance degrades
Real-world evaluation limitations: SceneCAD training set very small (~1k scenes), predominantly synthetic datasets, restricted to indoor scenes only
Incomplete comparison landscape: no comparison with other acceleration techniques (distillation, quantization, pruning) and no empirical comparison with other MTP approaches (Medusa, VocalNet)
Design choices lack thorough justification: τ=2 selected with minimal ablation, different thresholds (ϵ=0.90, 0.30, 0.50) appear arbitrary, no principled justification for binary cross-entropy loss

Insufficient analysis of critical findings: softmax-reliability correlation (Fig. 7) deserves deeper investigation; object detection shows lower α values than layout estimation with minimal explanation
Confidence head design concern: Table S4 shows training on first-head predictions vs. ground truth yields minimal difference, suggesting weak or uncertain confidence signal

Limited analysis of token filtering and failure modes: different token types and task-specific performance differences (layout vs. detection) insufficiently explained; failure cases relegated to supplementary
Lack of computational breakdown: overhead of confidence head inference not quantified; impact of pre-training then fine-tuning strategy unclear
